extracted.intended_audience: journalists, lawyers, students, and general readers researching defamation law
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive overview of legal standards, elements, defenses, jurisdictional differences, and practical issues in defamation (libel and slander) law as presented on a general-reference wiki page. Focuses on what constitutes defamation, available defenses, and how rules vary between jurisdictions and media (including the internet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of defamation (five essentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several sources state 'There are five essential elements to defamation: (1) The accusation is false; (2) it impeaches the subject's character; (3) it is published to a third person; (4) it damages the reputation of the subject; and (5) that the accusation is done intentionally or with fault such as wanton disregard of facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation (attributed to practice texts) is presented as the core checklist most jurisdictions consider when assessing a defamation claim: falsity, harmfulness to reputation, publication, and a required mental state/fault. Use this as a starting template but check local law for variations in wording and proof requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsity / provability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple sources: 'A statement can only be defamatory if it is false; therefore true statements of fact about others, regardless of the damage rendered, are not defamatory' and 'because the plaintiff must prove a statement is false in order to win an action in defamation, it is impossible to win an action in defamation if the statement, by its very nature, cannot be proven false.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsity is a threshold in many common-law jurisdictions: truth defeats defamation. Statements that cannot be proven true or false (rhetorical hyperbole, value judgments) are less likely to be actionable. Check jurisdictional exceptions (some places treat certain defamatory statements differently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact versus opinion distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The page emphasises that making a negative statement is not defamation 'unless the statement is false and represents something as a fact (for example, 'Vladik cheats on his taxes') rather than a personal opinion (for example, 'Vladik is a jerk').' It also notes the Supreme Court has ruled the First Amendment does not require recognition of an 'opinion privilege.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a statement, determine whether it is presented as a factual assertion (potentially actionable) or as opinion/rhetorical hyperbole (often non-actionable). However, U.S. constitutional law and other jurisdictions treat opinion privileges differently—examine local precedent (e.g., Milkovich, Hustler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel versus slander (form of publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional distinction: 'Libel refers to written defamatory statements; slander refers to oral statements. Libel encompasses communications occurring in 'physical form'... defamatory statements on records and computer tapes are considered libel rather than slander.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form affects procedural and sometimes substantive rules (e.g., preservation of proof, reputation of medium). Modern statutes and case law often collapse differences for online publications, treating persistent written online statements as libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and doctrinal statement: 'one famous 1734 case involving John Peter Zenger sowed the seed for the later establishment of truth as an absolute defence against libel charges.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where available, proving the truth of a challenged factual assertion is a complete defense. Jurisdictions differ on the scope of the truth defense and procedural burdens (who bears proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault standards and 'actual malice' for public figures
rubrics_metrics.description: References to New York Times Co. v. Sullivan and similar U.S. precedents indicate that for public officials (and in many cases public figures) the plaintiff must show higher fault (actual malice) rather than mere negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the plaintiff's status (private individual vs public official/figure). Public-figure plaintiffs usually must show 'actual malice' (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth) in U.S. law; other jurisdictions apply different fault standards. Always verify local case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages requirement and 'defamation per se' issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The page cites commentary that plaintiffs may need to plead and prove actual damages and warns 'Be Prepared to Plead (and Prove!) Actual Damages' in some contexts; other doctrines (defamation per se) can affect whether damages are presumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some categories of statements are actionable per se (presumed damages) in some jurisdictions, while in others plaintiffs must prove actual harm. Check local statutory and case law to know whether damages must be alleged and what proof is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication (third-party communication) and locus of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The classic element 'published to a third person' appears repeatedly. For online material, cases like Dow Jones v Gutnick are cited, reflecting the principle that publication can be where the material is received/read, which has implications for 'libel tourism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement must be communicated to someone other than the plaintiff and defendant. For internet cases, courts may treat publication as occurring where readers access the content — affecting jurisdiction and applicable law. Consider forum-shopping risks and choice-of-law rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges and recognized defenses (fair comment, opinion, qualified privilege)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article references 'Opinion and Fair Comment Privileges' and other protective doctrines; it also notes 'the First Amendment does not require recognition of an opinion privilege' in the U.S. and that defenses vary across systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common defenses include fair comment, opinion, absolute and qualified privilege (e.g., parliamentary or judicial proceedings), and statutory immunities. The availability and scope of each defense are jurisdiction-specific; evaluate context and whether the statement fits a protected category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal defamation and decriminalisation trends
rubrics_metrics.description: The page documents that some countries retain criminal defamation laws (lists many national penal codes) and cites reports/advocacy pushing for decriminalisation, noting risks to freedom of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware whether the jurisdiction criminalises defamation (possible fines, imprisonment) or treats it solely as a civil wrong; human-rights bodies and NGOs frequently advocate decriminalisation because of chilling effects. Check local statutes for penalties and procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate and group defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries discuss defamation of corporate entities ('Defamation of corporate entities in England') and scholarship on 'Group Libel', indicating that corporations and groups can be the subject of defamation claims in some jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the plaintiff is an individual, corporate entity, or group. Rules on group libel vary (e.g., whether a large group can claim individual reputational harm). Corporate plaintiffs may face different thresholds (e.g., need to show special damage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variation and choice of terms (tort/delict) and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The article emphasises wide cross-jurisdictional differences (use of 'delict' in some civil-law jurisdictions, differing substantive rules, references to national statutes and international instruments such as the European Convention and OSCE/UN reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume rules from one jurisdiction apply elsewhere: terminology, elements, defenses, and remedies vary. Consult local legislation, leading cases, and international human-rights guidance when working across borders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑SLAPP statutes and procedural protections
rubrics_metrics.description: References include California Code of Civil Procedure §425.16 and Ontario's 'Protection of Public Participation Act, 2015', and discussion of SLAPP (strategic lawsuits against public participation) concerns and responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑SLAPP laws provide procedures to dismiss suits aimed at chilling public participation; knowing whether such procedural protections exist is crucial when evaluating risk and relief strategies for speech-related suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and litigation outcomes (damages/injunctions/high awards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article cites high-profile awards (e.g., 'Firm Awarded $222.7 Million in a Libel Suit Vs. Dow Jones') and mentions courts awarding damages in libel suits, showing that remedies can include large monetary awards and other relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential remedies include compensatory damages, punitive damages in some jurisdictions, retractions, apologies, and injunctions. The scale and availability of remedies depend on jurisdictional rules and whether malice or other aggravating factors are proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special categories and protections (e.g., defamation of the deceased, insults at work)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page notes statutory provisions in some codes for defamation/calumny against deceased or absent persons (Swiss examples) and discusses workplace-related insults and related legal responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain jurisdictions create tailored offences or civil remedies for insults to the dead or protected categories; consider statutory text for any special categories and procedural implications.
